passages.t: A man and not a god
passages.happening:
God speaks to the ruler of Tyre. ‘Your heart is proud’, and he has claimed to sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea. ‘Yet you are a man and not a god, though you have regarded your heart as that of a god’ (verse 2). He thinks himself wiser than Daniel, and by his wisdom and trade he has piled up gold and silver, and his heart has grown proud because of his wealth (verses 3-5).

So God will bring foreigners against him, the most ruthless of nations, and he will die in the heart of the sea (verses 7-8). Will he still claim to be a god before those who kill him? ‘You will be only a man, not a god, in the hands of those who wound you’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The chapter does not name the king. According to Josephus, citing Phoenician records, the king during Nebuchadnezzar's siege was Ithobaal. Kings in the ancient Near East often claimed special closeness to the gods, and some were honored as divine.

The Daniel of verse 3 is spelled Dan'el, as in 14:14. Interpreters differ on whether he is the Daniel of the book of Daniel, a younger man in Babylon, or an ancient figure famed for wisdom, since a just king named Danel appears in texts from the Canaanite city of Ugarit.

The charge is plain: wealth made the king proud, and pride made him imagine he was more than human.
passages.later: ‘Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall’ (Proverbs 16:18). Isaiah pictured the king of Babylon saying, ‘I will make myself like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:14).
passages.asks: The king's wealth made him think he was a god. Ask where success has made you feel beyond the reach of anyone. And ask what it would mean to remember that you are only human.

passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to lament for the king of Tyre. ‘You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God’ (verses 12-13), adorned with every precious stone. ‘You were anointed as a guardian cherub’, on the holy mountain of God, walking among the fiery stones (verse 14). He was blameless from the day he was created ‘until wickedness was found in you’ (verse 15). Through his trade he was filled with violence, and God cast him from the mountain (verse 16). ‘Your heart grew proud of your beauty’ (verse 17), and fire consumed him (verse 18).

A short word follows against Sidon (verses 20-23). Then God promises that when he gathers Israel, ‘they will dwell securely, build houses, and plant vineyards’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The lament draws on pictures a priest knew well. Eden was the first sanctuary in Scripture. The cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life and were pictured on the ark. The mountain of God and the fiery stones suggest God's own dwelling. The precious stones recall the stones on the high priest's breastpiece.

Sidon, about twenty miles north, was the older of the two great Phoenician cities. Israel's history with Sidon was troubled: Jezebel, who promoted Baal worship in Israel, was the daughter of a king of the Sidonians.
passages.later: After the fall, God stationed cherubim ‘to guard the way to the tree of life’ (Genesis 3:24). Ahab married ‘Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians’ (1 Kings 16:31).
passages.hard:
Is the lament in verses 12 to 19 about Satan's fall?

The text's own horizon comes first. The lament is addressed to the king of Tyre, and the charges are those of chapters 26 and 27: pride, dishonest trade and violence (verses 16 and 18). The Eden imagery fits a human figure. The first human beings were placed in the garden, created good, and expelled when they reached for what belonged to God. Many interpreters read the lament as describing the king in the language of the first human fall, to say that his pride repeats Adam's and deserves the same exile. Others read it as the king's own self-image, a divine being in paradise, turned against him.

From early in the church's history, many Christians have read the passage as a picture of Satan's fall. Writers such as Tertullian and Origen applied it to the devil, often with Isaiah 14, and the reading remains common in popular teaching and in some evangelical scholarship. Its defenders argue that being in Eden, a guardian cherub, and blameless from creation goes beyond any human king, and that the prophet looks through the earthly ruler to the spiritual power behind his pride. Those who hesitate note that the New Testament never cites this passage of Satan, that the Hebrew of the cherub verses is uncertain, and that the passage aims at human arrogance. This site takes no side. Both readings agree on the lesson: pride that grasps at God's place ends in ruin.
passages.asks: The king was given beauty and wisdom and turned them into pride. Ask which of your gifts tempts you most toward pride. And ask how you might hold it as a gift instead.
